summary: Surveys the standard Internet security mechanisms that protocol designers can apply when building or reviewing a protocol. It explains that security must be designed in, and that the right mechanism depends on the structure of the protocol. It reviews several choices and explains the properties of each.

plainLanguage.summary: Before building a house, you pick the right locks for the doors and windows. This guide shows protocol builders the different kinds of locks available and what each is good at.

questions: what security mechanisms exist for internet protocols
how to choose security for a new protocol
which security mechanism should i use for a protocol
what does mandatory to implement mean
subtitle: An IAB guide to choosing among standard Internet security mechanisms, and to the ones to avoid.

tldr.problem: Protocols that lack built-in security cannot be fixed by good implementations alone, yet designers must pick from many mechanisms with different properties.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists the decision factors (threat model, mandatory-to-implement mechanisms, granularity, layer), then reviews standard mechanisms such as HMAC, IPsec, TLS, SASL, GSS-API, DNSSEC, S/MIME, OpenPGP, Kerberos and SSH, plus weak ones to avoid.
tldr.outcome: It is guidance, not a specification, and stresses that security must be designed in with the protocol rather than sprinkled on afterwards.

today: RFC 3631 is an Informational memo from the Internet Architecture Board, published in December 2003. The metadata lists no obsoleting or updating RFC, and its mechanism reviews reflect the state of the art at that time.

sections.title: Security Has to Be Designed In
sections.content:
The RFC divides Internet security compromises into classes from denial of service to host compromise. Flooding attacks are out of scope, and host compromise is usually an implementation flaw. But some compromises are made possible by the protocols themselves, and then no implementation can prevent them.

The IETF has developed standard mechanisms that can often supply the needed security, and the RFC gives guidance based on the IAB Security Architecture Workshop. It warns that security is an art, not a science, that mechanisms are not "magic pixie dust" to sprinkle on a finished protocol, and that no cryptography can rescue a protocol with flawed semantic assumptions.
sections.plainLanguage: You cannot add a good lock after the walls are built wrong. Safety has to be part of the plan from the start.

sections.title: Decision Factors
sections.content:
The most important factor is the threat model: who might attack what, and how. A public-information web site needs less protection than a major backbone router or a high-level Domain Name Server. Eavesdropping is a serious threat, and active attacks that insert or delete packets, including session hijacking after authentication completes, can be launched with off-the-shelf tools. The RFC says the default today should be the strongest cryptography available, since it often costs no more than weaker options.

It also covers mandatory-to-implement mechanisms. The IETF requires all protocols to provide appropriate security, even if first meant for a limited domain, because successful protocols end up used more widely. Mandatory means mandatory to implement, not necessarily to use, and an old weak mandatory algorithm is better disabled when a stronger one exists.

Two further factors are granularity (a whole network down to an individual user) and implementation layer. A lower layer protects more protocols but may protect each less well. A link-layer encryptor covers even ARP but only one link, while a signed email survives many gateways but protects only that one type of message.
sections.plainLanguage: First ask who might break in and what they want. A lemonade stand needs a smaller lock than a bank vault. Then decide how big a thing the lock covers.

sections.title: Standard Mechanisms for Authentication and Channels
sections.content:
The RFC reviews these standard mechanisms in turn.

  • One-time passwords (RFC 2289) are stronger than ordinary passwords, but guessing attacks may still work and logins expire after a set number of uses.
  • HMAC (RFC 2104) is the preferred shared-secret technique. It should be applied to every packet, since authenticating only the start of a TCP session leaves it open to theft. Simple keyed MD5 hashes, like the one in the BGP session mechanism of RFC 2385, are to be avoided in new protocols. SHA-1 is preferable to MD5 for HMAC.
  • IPsec protects all upper layers, typically host-to-host, host-to-gateway or gateway-to-gateway. It is transparent to applications but intrusive to the network stack, can conflict with NAT, and is the choice for VPN-like situations.
  • TLS gives an encrypted, authenticated channel over TCP. Applications generally must be converted individually, servers are normally authenticated by certificate, and users often click through warnings.
  • SASL negotiates an authentication and encryption mechanism over TCP. It pairs well with TLS: TLS authenticates the server and SASL authenticates clients.
  • GSS-API supplies opaque authentication tokens and, unlike SASL, works easily with UDP applications.
sections.plainLanguage: There are many kinds of locks. Some guard the whole road (IPsec), some guard one conversation (TLS), and some prove who you are with a secret you share.

sections.title: Signatures, Mail Security, Kerberos and SSH
sections.content:
DNSSEC digitally signs DNS records and protects against cache contamination. The RFC notes it was not widely deployed at the time of writing. Security/Multipart (RFC 1847) is the preferred framework for protecting email, used by both S/MIME and OpenPGP, and is one form of "object security".

Digital signatures are strong for challenge/response because servers need only the public key. A client should never sign the exact challenge it receives, and DSA needs good random numbers or the private key can be recovered.

S/MIME relies on X.509 certificates and a few root CAs, which needs a deployed public key infrastructure but suits corporate settings. OpenPGP uses a "web of trust" that works without infrastructure but expects more user knowledge. Kerberos lets two parties authenticate and exchange keying material through tickets and authenticators, and has known vulnerabilities but can be used securely. SSH works much like TLS, is optimized for terminal-like remote connections, and can tunnel other protocols.

Firewalls are also discussed. They cannot stop inside attacks, weaken as users tunnel through them, and hurt the end-to-end model, so they work best as one part of a total security structure.
sections.plainLanguage: Signing a letter proves it came from you. Mail tools, ticket systems and secure remote logins each use that idea in a different way.

sections.title: Insecurity Mechanisms to Avoid
sections.content:
The RFC calls out common mechanisms that are "part of the problem".

  • Plaintext passwords are the most common and the weakest. Unprotected they are completely unacceptable, and even over encryption the server sees them. With a dictionary, 20-30% of passwords can be guessed in most environments.
  • Address-based authentication can work only in tightly controlled settings. Threats include ARP spoofing, IP address spoofing, routing table corruption and source-routed packets.
  • Name-based authentication has all those problems plus attacks on the DNS. DNSSEC helps with the DNS part but does nothing for the reliability of the underlying address.
sections.plainLanguage: Telling someone your password out loud, or letting anyone who knows the right street address walk in, are bad locks. Do not use them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: No security mechanism is perfect, and any network-based mechanism can be defeated by compromise of the endpoints. Each mechanism has its own limits. A decision to adopt one should weigh all its failure modes against the risk to the endpoint of a security failure. The RFC has no IANA considerations.
sections.plainLanguage: Even the best lock fails if the burglar is already inside the house. So think about what could go wrong with each choice.
